questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: secure container runtime, init containers, config-driven rollouts, resource limits, probes, graceful termination, disruption budgets, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- SecurityContext and podSecurityContext for non-root operation
- InitContainer usage and seed data from ConfigMap
- Rolling restart triggers via checksum/config annotation
- Probes and termination settings
- PodDisruptionBudget and NetworkPolicy integration

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal patch skeleton (conceptual)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: worker
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "<computed-from-configmap>"
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: myorg/worker:latest
          securityContext:
            runAsUser: 1000
            runAsGroup: 1000
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
          env: []
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "128Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
      initContainers:
        - name: seed-data
          image: busybox
          command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /config/bootstrap/* /data/" ]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: worker-data-pvc
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: worker-config
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you automate the checksum calculation for the config annotation in CI/CD?
- How would you verify rollback behavior in a live cluster without affecting production traffic?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design a one-off reconciliation Job that interacts with external services, ensures idempotent processing via a fingerprint, and properly configures InitContainers, Secrets, and backoff behavior. It also checks handling of PVC-mounted data and rollback planning.


## Key Concepts

- Kubernetes Job with backoff and deadline
- InitContainer for bootstrap tooling
- PVC mounting and data access in a one-off task
- yq for YAML extraction
- Idempotent design via server fingerprint key
- Secret and ConfigMap usage for credentials and endpoints
- Rollback and observability considerations


## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: data-ingest-audit-reconcile
spec:
  backoffLimit: 4
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 900
  template:
    metadata:
      name: data-ingest-audit-reconcile
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: reconciler
        image: your-registry/audit-client:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "set -e; /bin/reconcile.sh /data/manifests.yaml"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: manifests
          mountPath: /data
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq && curl -L -o /usr/local/bin/yq https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/releases/download/v4.9.6/yq_linux_amd64 && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/yq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: manifests
          mountPath: /data
      restartPolicy: Never
      volumes:
      - name: manifests
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: data-manifests
      imagePullSecrets:
      - name: regcred
```


## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test idempotency in CI/CD?
- How would you scale this for larger manifest sets without timeouts?
- How would you monitor and rollback on failure?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests knowledge of Namespace-scoped quotas and defaults, a core CKAD topic. It also checks YAML correctness and practical validation steps.

## Key Concepts

- ResourceQuota structure and hard limits
- LimitRange defaults and constraints
- Impact on deployments and pod scheduling
- Validation commands and monitoring

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-a-quota
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "20"
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: "8Gi"
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: "16Gi"
```

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: team-a-defaults
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
  - default:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: "128Mi"
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "50m"
      memory: "64Mi"
    type: Container
```


Assesses ability to choreograph ephemeral canaries using core CKAD primitives: templated Deployment from ConfigMap, secret-based auth, logs via PVC, init containers, probes, and namespace-scoped NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts

- ConfigMap templating for Deployment

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-tester
spec:
  schedule: "*/20 * * * *"

    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
            - name: install-tools
              image: alpine:3.18
              command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
```

## Why This Is Asked
This tests practical CKAD pattern: file-driven config synchronization, idempotent object creation, secret management, and namespace-scoped network policy.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer tooling, kubectl in-cluster, ConfigMap/Secret management, TLS sidecar, NetworkPolicy scoping.
- Cadence-based reconciliation and minimal YAML skeletons for CKAD.

## Code Example
```javascript
# Minimal skeleton for a Deployment that performs config sync
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-sync
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: config-sync
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.17
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache jq curl kubectl"]
      containers:
        - name: main
          image: my-registry/config-sync:latest
          env:
            - name: SYNC_INTERVAL
              value: "300s"
      volumes:
        - name: config
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: config-pvc
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 10
        periodSeconds: 5
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 30
        periodSeconds: 10
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you secure the TLS sidecar and rotate certs without restarting pods?
- How would you test reconciliation and conflict resolution between file changes and cluster objects?

This question tests the ability to operate within a namespace context while working with core Kubernetes primitives: ConfigMaps for configuration, Secrets for sensitive data, and a controller-like process to automate cleanup tasks. It also assesses knowledge of observability (logging to PVC), container tooling (InitContainers), health checks, and network security.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped RBAC for job listing and deletion
- ConfigMap-driven TTL configuration
- Secrets for API key storage
- Kubernetes API access patterns (list, watch, delete Jobs)
- PVC-backed logging
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- Readiness and liveness probes
- NetworkPolicy for egress restrictions

## Trade-offs
- **Per-namespace vs. cluster-wide**: A per-namespace deployment provides isolation and TTL flexibility per namespace but increases resource overhead. A cluster-wide operator is more efficient but less flexible.
- **Polling vs. watching**: Polling is simpler to implement but introduces latency; watching is more efficient but adds complexity.
- **Push vs. pull for digests**: Sending digests immediately provides real-time visibility but increases API calls; batching reduces load but delays information.

## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical CKAD skills: autoscaling, robustness, and upgrade safety in real workloads.

## Key Concepts

- Deployment resources and probes
- HorizontalPodAutoscaler (autoscale on CPU)
- PodDisruptionBudget for maintenance safety
- Observability: kubectl top, metrics-server

## Code Example

```yaml
# Deployment patch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: collector
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: collector
        image: collector:latest
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 15
```

```yaml
# HPA
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: collector-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: collector
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 6
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 60
```

```yaml
# PodDisruptionBudget
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: collector-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: collector
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you verify HPA behavior under a synthetic load step?
- What changes if workloads are bursty and you want per-pod CPU caps?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design a namespace-scoped TLS gateway leveraging CRD, InitContainer, Secrets, and a ready path tied to certificate availability.

## Key Concepts

- CustomResourceDefinition for per-namespace gateways
- InitContainer fetching TLS certs via Vault-like API
- Secrets mounted into gateway for TLS material
- Readiness/Liveness linked to cert presence/expiry; logs to a PVC

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: tlsgateways.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              serviceName:
                type: string
              port:
                type: integer
              hostname:
                type: string
              apiTokenSecret:
                type: string
```

```yaml
apiVersion: example.com/v1
kind: TLSGateway
metadata:
  name: my-service-gateway
  namespace: default
spec:
  serviceName: my-service
  port: 443
  hostname: app.example.com
  apiTokenSecret: tlsgateway-token
```

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: tls-gateway
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: tls-gateway
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: tls-gateway
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: fetch-certs
        image: curlimages/curl:8.1
        command: ["sh", "-c", "curl -sS http://vault.example/api/cert -o /certs/tls.crt"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: certs
          mountPath: /certs
      containers:
      - name: envoy
        image: envoyproxy/envoy:v1.23.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 443
        volumeMounts:
        - name: certs
          mountPath: /etc/envoy/certs
      volumes:
      - name: certs
        secret:
          secretName: tlsgateway-certs
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you handle cert rotation cadence and revocation?
- What RBAC would you implement for the InitContainer to access the API token?

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD-level design and debugging of StatefulSets, bootstrapping, and network policies under real constraints.

## Key Concepts
- StatefulSet with stable identity and PVC
- headless Service and partitioned rolling updates
- InitContainer for bootstrapping
- PodDisruptionBudget and readiness/liveness probes
- Resource quotas and NetworkPolicy bounds

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: cache-svc
  labels:
    app: cache
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: cache
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: cache
spec:
  serviceName: cache-svc
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cache
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: seed
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "echo seed > /data/.seed"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
      containers:
      - name: cache
        image: redis:7
        ports:
        - containerPort: 6379
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: "/ready", port: 6379}
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: "/live", port: 6379}
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: cache-pvc
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: cache
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: cache-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cache
```

This question evaluates a candidate's ability to design production-ready, per-namespace observability data flows—a critical skill for platform engineers and SREs. questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses the ability to design a namespace-scoped canary workflow using standard CKAD primitives: CronJob, ConfigMaps, and Deployment rolling updates. It also tests observability knowledge via PVC-backed logs, status tracking patterns, and security awareness through NetworkPolicy and InitContainer usage.

## Key Concepts
- **ConfigMaps**: canary-config holds dynamic parameters (targetImage, canaryPercent); canary-status records rollout history and last-promotion timestamps
- **CronJob**: Provides periodic reconciliation that checks configuration and triggers conditional updates
- **Deployment RollingUpdate**: maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 ensures controlled, non-disruptive updates
- **Traffic Shifting**: Routes a configurable percentage of traffic to canary pods for gradual exposure
- **InitContainer**: Ensures jq availability for JSON parsing within the job
- **Probes**: Readiness gates ensure traffic only reaches healthy pods; liveness checks restart unhealthy instances
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricts namespace egress to approved registries only
- **PVC**: Persists job logs for debugging and audit trails

## Trade-offs
- **Pros**: Fully Kubernetes-native with no external dependencies; ConfigMap history provides auditability; automatic promotion reduces manual intervention
- **Cons**: Namespace-scoped only; NetworkPolicy requires CNI support; jq dependency increases image size; ConfigMaps lack built-in validation

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests knowledge of namespace-scoped governance primitives (LimitRange, ResourceQuota) and how defaults affect scheduling, QoS, and multi-tenant fairness in CKAD.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace scoping
- LimitRange defaultRequests/defaultLimits
- ResourceQuota hard limits
- Pod scheduling under quotas
- Impact on autoscaling and experimentation

## Code Example
```yaml
# Namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: test-ns
---
# LimitRange
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  limits:
  - default:
      cpu: 200m
      memory: 256Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
    type: Container
---
# ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: resource-quota
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "10"
    requests.cpu: "1"
    requests.memory: 1Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 2Gi
---
# Deployment (inherits defaults)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: sample-app
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: sample-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: sample-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:latest
```

## Trade-offs
**Advantages:**
- Prevents resource starvation across namespaces
- Enforces fair resource distribution
- Automatic defaults reduce configuration errors
- Provides cost control boundaries

**Considerations:**
- Too restrictive limits can hinder scaling
- Default limits may be overprovisioned for small workloads
- ResourceQuota refusals require manual quota increases
- May impact autoscaling behavior if quotas are too tight

**Best Practices:**
- Set conservative defaults but allow overrides
- Monitor quota utilization regularly
- Use separate quotas for production vs development
- Consider pod priority classes for critical workloads

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to compose namespace-scoped resources and practical config/secret usage.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap and Secret usage in a Deployment
- InitContainer for dependency install
- Sidecar for TLS cert rotation
- Readiness/Liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress
- PVC mounting and per-namespace isolation

## Code Example
```yaml
# YAML skeleton
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
  namespace: example-ns
data:
  ENDPOINT: "http://data-portal:8443/api/v1/ingest"
  MODE: "batch"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: api-credentials
  namespace: example-ns
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: collector
  password: s3cr3t
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: data-collector
  namespace: example-ns
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: data-collector
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: data-collector
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: init-deps
          image: python:3.11
          command: ["bash","-lc","pip install -r requirements.txt"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      containers:
        - name: collector
          image: my-reg/collector:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: app-config
            - secretRef:
                name: api-credentials
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
            - name: tls
              mountPath: /tls
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: data-pvc
        - name: tls
          secret:
            secretName: tls-certs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test TLS rotation in a cluster?
- What changes to support multiple namespaces with shared TLS secrets?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills for multi-namespace automation, pod networking, and safe secret handling via Secrets and ConfigMaps.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob in a Namespace; PVC mounts
- InitContainer installation; jq usage
- Secret/ConfigMap usage; status tracking
- NetworkPolicy scoping; per-namespace egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: metrics-watcher
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
          - name: collector
            image: registry.example/metrics-collector:latest
            volumeMounts:
            - name: metrics-pvc
              mountPath: /metrics
            - name: logs-pvc
              mountPath: /logs
            env:
            - name: ENDPOINT
              value: "https://metrics-portal:9090/api/v1/digest"
            - name: API_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: metrics-secret
                  key: api-token
          initContainers:
          - name: install-tools
            image: appropriate/curl
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache jq && mkdir -p /logs"]
          volumes:
          - name: metrics-pvc
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: metrics-pvc
          - name: logs-pvc
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you rotate the API token without restarting the CronJob?
- What are trade-offs of using a CronJob for real-time metrics vs. a DaemonSet collector?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD patterns for per-namespace resources, log pipelines, and robust error handling with limited tooling.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped Deployments and PVCs
- InitContainers for bootstrap tooling
- ConfigMap/Secret for endpoint and credentials
- Simple in-Pod state via streaming tail and per-minute aggregation
- DLQ on PVC for failed forwards
- Readiness/Liveness probes

## Code Example

```yaml
# skeleton Deployment (high level)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-forwarder
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-forwarder
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: installer
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
      containers:
        - name: forwarder
          image: some-forwarder:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            - name: dlq
              mountPath: /logs/dlq
          env:
            - name: ENDPOINT
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: log-forwarder-config
                  key: ENDPOINT
            - name: API_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: log-forwarder-secret
                  key: API_TOKEN
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-pvc
        - name: dlq
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-dlq-pvc
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you scale and parallelize across namespaces?
- How to secure endpoint access and rotate API_TOKEN?
